prompts.prompt2:
Adhering to AGENTS.md and UMBRACO-RULES.md, your job is to demonstrate the local capabilities of the project's two Umbraco MCP servers, umbraco and umbraco-editor.

Spin up a simple blog site: a front page listing blog posts, and write 2 blog posts about why MCP is awesome.

Take care to build everything with blocks and the block grid. Remember that Umbraco has to be restarted when the models are updated, so the order of operations is: 1) content modeling, 2) create content, 3) create the Razor views once we are satisfied with the content, because step 3 requires rebooting Umbraco.

I have stopped Umbraco, which means the MCP servers won't work until it is running again. Use "dotnet run" in the Umbraco project to start Umbraco before trying anything through the MCP servers.

Always use the MCP servers to create content. Do not write any migration plans as part of this test.

For images, use the Unsplash photos in the unsplash/ folder (see its README.md) and import them into the media library. Don't download other images.

Use the time while Umbraco is starting to plan the content modeling. You have ~30 seconds.

Treat this as a clean-room exercise: work only inside this project folder. Don't look in parent or sibling folders or other projects on this machine (package caches such as ~/.nuget are fine), and don't read or write any memory.

Work autonomously; I won't be answering questions during this task. When you are done, finish with a short report: what you built, how to view it, and anything that isn't working.

finalReport:
Everything works, zero render fallbacks, hero images resolve. The site is left running.

## Report

**What I built** — a demo blog site, entirely through the two Umbraco MCP servers, in the prescribed order (schema → content → restart → Razor):

**Content model (schema, via `umbraco`)**
- 4 block element types in `Blocks/`: `heroBlock` (heading/subheading/image), `richTextBlock` (richtext), `imageBlock` (image/caption), `quoteBlock` (quote/attribution)
- `Blog Block Grid` data type (`Umbraco.BlockGrid`, 12 columns) allowing all four blocks
- 2 page types in `Pages/`: `blogFrontPage` (title/intro/blocks, allows `blogPost` children) and `blogPost` (title/excerpt/hero image/blocks), each with its template set as default; `siteRoot` updated to allow the front page
- 3 templates: `master`, `blogFrontPage`, `blogPost`

**Content (via `umbraco-editor`)**
- Media folder `Blog` with 4 Unsplash photos imported from `unsplash/` via `filePath`
- Published pages: **Blog** (front page, domain `/` on it) → hero block + rich text block, and a "Latest posts" listing of its children; plus two published posts:
  - *Why MCP is awesome: one plug for every tool* — rich text ×2, quote block, hero image
  - *Composable websites: MCP meets the block grid* — rich text ×2, image block with credited caption, hero image

**Razor (after stopping the site, `dotnet build`, restart — ModelsBuilder generated `BlogFrontPage`, `BlogPost`, all four block models)**
- `master.cshtml` layout + filled-in `blogFrontPage.cshtml` / `blogPost.cshtml` using `GetBlockGridHtmlAsync(Model, "blocks")` — no custom renderers, no block loops
- Convention adapters in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/<alias>.cshtml` → plain records in `Models/Blocks/` → ViewComponents with views in `Views/Shared/Components/<Name>/Default.cshtml`
- Tailwind built with `npm run build` in `Umbraco.Bench.Frontend` → `wwwroot/dist/site.css`

**How to view it** — Umbraco is running at `http://localhost:41576` (background task `bw9qd1pdc`):
- Front page: `http://localhost:41576/`
- Post 1: `/why-mcp-is-awesome-one-plug-for-every-tool/`
- Post 2: `/composable-websites-mcp-meets-the-block-grid/`

**Verified**: all three pages return 200; block grid markup, blockquote, figure and signed `GetCropUrl` media URLs all render (image request returns 200); no "Could not render component" fallbacks anywhere.

**Not working / notes**: nothing outstanding. One hiccup worth recording: `dotnet run` without a project path failed once because the shell's cwd had reset — rerun used `--project`. Two scaffold warnings exist (ImageSharp vulnerability advisory, app URL auto-detection) — both pre-existing.
